reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

reading.ours: stamp the identity with the frame number and push it onto a plain array
reading.floor: add the identity to a Set<identity>, which dedups by membership
reading.caveat: THE PUBLISHED CLAIM, REBUILT — 1024 identities, every one of them marked once per flush, and the batch then WALKED rather than delivered, which is what the published microbench did ("mark + iterate, nothing else") and is the only way this row can be about the container. Both arms owe the same M deliveries and the delivery is the same shipped code either way, so putting it in would add one constant to both halves of the ratio — and a constant added to both halves only pulls a ratio toward 1, hardest where the margin is largest. `subscribe.deliver-vs-direct-call` prices delivery on its own, so a reader who wants the per-mark-plus-delivery figure can add the two rather than have them silently mixed here. `mark`'s own `changedInFrame` stamp is on neither arm for the same reason — every design keeps it, whatever it queues into. The only difference between the two bodies is therefore the container the batch is kept in. What the Set BUYS, and it is not nothing: dedup and membership are one operation, there is no per-identity word to keep in step, and the invariant the flag design has to hold by hand — the identity is in the batch iff its stamp says so — cannot be broken, so it cannot drop an update or double-deliver. The blog post pays for the speed with that invariant and says so. RESIDUALS, and both push the same way: every mark here is a FIRST mark, so our stamp never takes its early return and the Set never probes an entry it already holds — the arrangement least favourable to the stamp, since a repeat mark is a field compare for us and a full hash probe for the Set, and `OIMDB.mark` records that five marks in six of a real batch are repeats. And the shipped stamp is a FRAME NUMBER, not the boolean the post measured, so no reset pass over the delivered batch is needed at all; the post's arm paid one store per delivered carrier that this one does not. The first understates our margin, the second means this arm is cheaper than the one the ~4x was measured on.

reading.ours: stamp and push — 64 of 1024 identities dirty per flush
reading.floor: Set.add — 64 of 1024 identities dirty per flush
reading.caveat: THE POST'S SECOND COLUMN. Everything the all-dirty row says applies unchanged; what differs is that a flush now delivers 64 identities instead of 1024, so the two containers are compared at a size a real interactive frame reaches rather than at a bulk load. What the Set BUYS is what it bought above, plus one thing that only shows here: its `clear()` is proportional to what was in it, so a sparse flush costs it almost nothing, where a boolean-flag design would have to walk the delivered batch to reset flags whatever its size. The shipped stamp does neither. THE WINDOW MOVES — each flush takes the next 64 identities rather than the same 64 — so neither arm is measured on a working set that has settled into L1 in a way the other's has not; both walk the whole population every 16 flushes. Direction: as above, and the first-mark-only arrangement understates our margin here too.

reading.ours: stamp the identity with the frame number and push it onto a plain array
reading.floor: keep the stamp in a Map<identity, frame> beside a plain array queue
reading.caveat: THE ARM THAT LOSES TO THE ONE IT WAS MEANT TO REPLACE, which is why it is worth a row of its own. This is the design proposed whenever "do not write engine bookkeeping onto the caller's objects" is the argument, and what it BUYS is exactly that: the identity carries no `queuedInFrame` word, nothing on it can be corrupted by a caller or by a second database, and the whole batch state can be thrown away at once. It is also the strictly WORSE half of the trade against the Set beside it — it keeps the array push AND pays a hash probe to read the stamp and a second to write it, where the Set pays one probe for dedup, membership and insertion together. Read this ratio beside the Set row above rather than on its own: both are measured against the same shipped arm in the same arrangement, which is what makes the two rejected designs comparable when their own two numbers come from different processes. THE MAP IS PERSISTENT and holds frame numbers rather than being cleared per flush, which is the cheapest honest form of this design — no rehash, no clear, no growth. Direction: in the rejected design's favour.

reading.ours: stamp and push — 64 of 1024 identities dirty per flush
reading.floor: Map<identity, frame> beside an array — 64 of 1024 dirty per flush
reading.caveat: THE SIDE MAP AT AN INTERACTIVE BATCH SIZE. Everything the all-dirty side-map row says holds; what this one adds is the case the design is usually argued for — a small batch out of a large population, where the map holds 1024 live entries and only 64 of them are probed. If the two side-map rows differ by much more than the two Set rows do, the difference is the map's working set rather than its per-mark cost, and that is a fact about the design and not about the measurement. What it BUYS is what it buys above: nothing of ours on the caller's object. Direction: the persistent map is the cheapest form of the rejected design, and the window moves so neither arm is measured on an unnaturally hot 64 rows.

reading.ours: call every subscriber and let the field closure early-return — 1 of 4 fires
reading.floor: consult a subscriber→column map first and skip the call — 1 of 4 fires
reading.caveat: ONE OPERATION IS ONE SUBSCRIBER CONSIDERED, not one delivery: four field subscriptions sit on each identity, one column moved, so three of the four must be filtered out and the ratio is per handler. BOTH ARMS RUN THE SHIPPED `OIMSubscriberStore.deliver` — the settled list, the disposal re-check, the buffer, the try/catch — and ours runs the shipped `db.subscribeToField` closures unmodified (`OIMDB.ts:952-963`); only the rejected filter is written here, as the `tell` override the shipped class documents as its variation seam. What the map BUYS: the call never happens, so a subscriber that does not care costs no frame; who wants what is data rather than something sealed inside a closure, which a devtool could list and a delivery could in principle use to skip whole groups without touching them; and the identity needs no `movedFields` array at all. RESIDUALS. Ours reads `slot.movedInFrame` against `db.frame.number` before it even looks at the column, which the map design does not need because delivery already established that the identity moved — a genuine ours-only cost, counted. The map arm is handed what moved once, outside the clock, where a real one would store it per delivery. And `deliver`'s own `this.tell` call site sees two receiver classes in this one process, so it is polymorphic for BOTH arms — an instrument effect paid equally, which pulls the ratio toward 1 and therefore shrinks whichever margin is real.

reading.ours: call every subscriber and let the field closure early-return — 3 of 4 fire
reading.floor: consult a subscriber→column map first and skip the call — 3 of 4 fire
reading.caveat: THE OTHER END OF THE ONE VARIABLE THAT DECIDES THIS, and the reason the row above must not be quoted alone. Three columns moved, so three of the four subscribers are owed their call and only one is filtered: everything the map saves by not calling is gone, and it still pays its lookup on all four. Ours pays a longer `indexOf` in return — the moved list has three entries here rather than one, and our filter scans it — so the two designs move toward each other from both sides. If the map is ahead in the 3-of-4-skipped row and behind in this one, the honest statement of the decision is a crossover in the skip fraction and not a speed-up, and the shipped choice is then an argument about which fraction a real screen sits at (a component watching one column of a row that moved for another reason is the common case, which is the row above). Every residual named in that row applies here unchanged.

reading.ours: push the marked identity onto the frame list; deliver the list — 1024 subscribed, 10 dirty
reading.floor: stamp only; at the frame, scan all 1024 and deliver those stamped this frame
reading.caveat: THE SPARSE END, WHICH IS WHERE AN INTERACTIVE FRAME LIVES: a keystroke moves one row of a mounted list, not all of them. Ours per frame: 10 marks, each paying a stamp compare and store, a `subscribers` field read, an `isEmpty` call, the delivery stamp and an array push — then a walk of 10. The scan per frame: 10 marks of ONE STORE each and then 1024 stamp comparisons. What the scan BUYS is real and is the reason it keeps being proposed: the write path loses its push, its second stamp and its emptiness question, so the hottest path in the engine gets shorter; there is no list to allocate, recycle, bound or double-buffer (`PENDING_KEEP_AT_MOST` and the two swapped arrays stop existing); and a mark cannot be lost by any list bookkeeping because there is no list. RESIDUALS. Both arms deliver through the shipped `OIMSubscriberStore.deliver`, exactly M times each, so delivery is not in the difference. Our mark carries the emptiness question that the scan design answers by construction — counted against us, correctly. The scan's mark is an unconditional store with no dedup, which is the leanest form the design has and is what it should be measured as. NEITHER ARM DELIVERS: both owe the same M deliveries of the same shipped code, and a constant added to both halves of a ratio only pulls it toward 1. `subscribe.deliver-vs-direct-call` prices delivery on its own.

reading.ours: push and deliver the list — 1024 subscribed, 102 dirty
reading.floor: stamp only, then scan all 1024 — 102 dirty
reading.caveat: TEN PER CENT, which is the point of this table and not a filler row: it is between the fraction where the list wins by an order of magnitude and the fraction where the scan takes the lead, so it is what says WHERE the crossover is rather than only that there is one. A batch load into a mounted screen — a page of search results replacing a page — is roughly here. What the scan buys and every residual are as stated in the 1% row; nothing about the two bodies changes but M.

reading.ours: push and deliver the list — 1024 subscribed, 512 dirty
reading.floor: stamp only, then scan all 1024 — 512 dirty
reading.caveat: THE ROW WHERE WE EXPECT TO LOSE, and it is here for that reason. With half the population dirty the scan walks 1024 stamps to find 512 deliveries while we pay per-write bookkeeping 512 times, and the remembered figure has the scan ahead by about 1.18x. THAT IS THE WHOLE CASE FOR THE DECISION AND NOT AGAINST IT: the loss is bounded — the scan can never beat us by more than the per-write bookkeeping, because at M = K it is doing our work minus the push — while the win at the sparse end is unbounded in K, since the scan pays for every subscriber that did not move. A design that loses at most ~1.18x and wins up to an order of magnitude is chosen on the shape of the payoff, not on any one of these four numbers. If this row comes back much WORSE than 1.18x, the bookkeeping is heavier than remembered and that is a real finding about the write path. Residuals as in the 1% row.

reading.ours: push and deliver the list — 8192 subscribed, 82 dirty
reading.floor: stamp only, then scan all 8192 — 82 dirty
reading.caveat: THE SAME FRACTION AS THE FIRST ROW, EIGHT TIMES THE POPULATION, which is the only way to show that the scan's cost is set by what is SUBSCRIBED and not by what changed. Our per-frame cost should barely move between this row and the 1k-1pct row (82 marks against 10, and no walk of the other 8110); the scan's should grow by roughly eight. A virtualised table with a subscription per row, a chat with a subscription per message, any screen that mounts thousands of readers and touches a handful per frame is this row. What the scan buys and the residuals are as in the 1% row; nothing changes but K.

reading.ours: write, mark the dependent once, recompute it at the frame — 1 write per node per frame
reading.floor: write, recompute the dependent immediately — 1 write per node per frame
reading.caveat: THE ROW WHERE WE EXPECT TO LOSE, AND THE ONE THAT SPEED CANNOT DECIDE. At one write per node per frame there is nothing to coalesce: both arms recompute once, and ours has additionally paid a stamp, a queue push and a drain to arrange it. Expect somewhere between 1.0x and 2.5x against us, and the closer this row is to 1.0x the cheaper the mechanism is when it is doing nothing. WHAT EAGER BUYS: the value is current the instant the write returns, so a reader needs no flush and no mental model of a frame; there is no queue, no stamp and no drain; and a node that nobody reads is never computed at all. WHAT NO RATIO IN THIS FILE PRICES, and it is the actual reason for the decision: on a diamond — A feeding B and C, D reading both — the eager arm recomputes D once per path and its FIRST run reads one fresh parent and one stale one. That is a value that never should have existed, delivered to whoever is watching, and it is a correctness failure rather than a slow one. Coalescing is what makes the graph settle before anything downstream runs. A reader who takes this row as an argument for eager has taken half the argument. RESIDUALS: both arms write through the same compare-gated field store, written out twice rather than shared, so neither pays a call the other does not; the shipped engine additionally orders the drain by level and gates each node on equality before waking anything downstream, and neither of those is in this arm — so our real mechanism costs MORE than what is measured here, and this ratio understates the loss.

reading.ours: write, mark once, recompute at the frame — 4 writes per node per frame
reading.floor: write, recompute immediately — 4 writes per node per frame
reading.caveat: PAST THE BREAK-EVEN, WHICH IS THE CLAIM BEING CHECKED: the remembered statement is that coalescing pays from more than one write per node per frame, so this row is the first that should sit below 1.0x. Ours does four marks — one full and three ending on the stamp's early return — and one recompute. Eager does four recomputes. Two writes to one row between two paints is not exotic: a server patch followed by a local edit, a form field and its validation, an optimistic write and its confirmation. What eager buys, and what no ratio prices, are stated in the 1-write row and are unchanged by the write count. Residuals as there.

reading.ours: write, mark once, recompute at the frame — 20 writes per node per frame
reading.floor: write, recompute immediately — 20 writes per node per frame
reading.caveat: THE FAR END, AND ITS MAGNITUDE IS A PROPERTY OF THE NODE AND NOT OF THE ENGINE. Ours does 20 marks and one recompute; eager does 20 recomputes. The ratio is therefore bounded above by 20 and reaches it only as the recompute grows large against the marking; the node here is deliberately CHEAP — one field read and a `.length` — so this row is the LOWER end of what coalescing is worth at 20 writes, and the row after it takes the same arrangement with a node worth computing. Quoting a single headline multiple for coalescing without naming the node it was measured over is the error this pair of rows exists to stop. What eager buys, and the correctness argument no ratio prices, are stated in the 1-write row.

reading.ours: write, mark once, recompute a 16-row derivation at the frame — 20 writes per node per frame
reading.floor: write, recompute the 16-row derivation immediately — 20 writes per node per frame
reading.caveat: THE SAME TWENTY WRITES OVER A NODE THAT ACTUALLY COSTS SOMETHING — a total over sixteen rows, which is what a derived value on a screen usually is (a sum in a footer, a count of what matches, a joined label). 256 nodes of 16 rows each; a write moves one row of a group and invalidates that group's node. Read against the row above, THE PAIR ANSWERS THE INDEPENDENCE QUESTION: the BREAK-EVEN stays at more than one write per node per frame whatever the node costs, because at one write both arms compute exactly once and only our bookkeeping separates them — but the SIZE of the win past the break-even is set almost entirely by the recompute, since coalescing saves 19 recomputes and nothing else. Two rows are the fewest that can show that; one would have been quoted as a headline. What eager buys, and the diamond argument that no ratio prices, are as stated in the 1-write row — and they matter MORE here, since a costlier node is usually a node with more parents.
